title: Symphony No. 4 in D minor
hook: Four movements played without a break and built from the same few ideas, from a dark beginning to a blazing D major.

painting.title: Fishing by Torchlight on the Krøderen
painting.pairingNote: A boat crosses a dark lake under moonlit clouds, lit by one torch; painted in 1851 by two Norwegians of the Düsseldorf school, in the city and the year in which Schumann, its new music director, rewrote his D minor symphony.

facts: Schumann wrote the symphony in 1841 in Leipzig, the year after he married the pianist Clara Wieck, straight after his *Spring* Symphony. He is said to have given the score to Clara on her birthday, 13 September 1841. It was first played at the Leipzig Gewandhaus on 6 December 1841, conducted by the orchestra’s leader, Ferdinand David, but it made little impression and Schumann put it aside.

Ten years later, in 1851, as music director in Düsseldorf, he revised it thoroughly: he made the orchestra fuller, tightened the links between the movements and changed the tempo marks from Italian to German. He conducted the new version in Düsseldorf, and it was published in 1853. Because two more symphonies had appeared in between, it became his No. 4.

The four movements are played without a break, and they share their themes: a melody from the slow introduction returns in the slow movement, a violin solo from the slow movement becomes the trio of the scherzo, and the finale grows out of the first movement’s main theme. Schumann had thought of calling the work a “symphonic fantasy”.
Johannes Brahms preferred the lighter original of 1841 and had it published in 1891, against Clara’s objections. Most orchestras play the 1851 version, as in this recording.
bigPicture.inOneLine: darkness and a restless struggle (I), a sad song with a violin’s garland (II), a stamping dance and a gentle trio (III), and a slow awakening into a bright, fast finale in D major (IV).

movements.heading: Ziemlich langsam – Lebhaft
movements.summary: A slow, dark introduction (“rather slow”) gathers speed and breaks into a fast movement (“lively”) built almost entirely on one short, restless figure. Instead of returning to its opening as a classical [[sonata-form|sonata form]] would, the movement presses on, finds new themes in the middle and ends in D major. It leads straight into the second movement.

mainIdeas.name: The introduction theme
mainIdeas.description: a long, winding melody in the violins, rising and falling in small steps, over a held bass note.

mainIdeas.name: The main figure of the *Lebhaft*
mainIdeas.description: a quick, circling run of notes in the violins, repeated again and again.

mainIdeas.name: Two new themes in the middle
mainIdeas.description: a loud, stabbing call with heavy chords, and a broad, singing tune.

stops.hear: A held note for the whole orchestra, then a slow, winding melody in the violins
stops.happening: The introduction. This melody will come back in the second movement

stops.hear: The winding melody quickens and grows louder
Fast and restless: the violins race round a short figure, the whole orchestra pushing behind
stops.happening: The *Lebhaft* begins with its main theme

stops.hear: The fast music starts again from its beginning
The racing figure moves through new keys, more urgently
Loud, hammered chords and a sharp call in the brass
stops.happening: A new idea in the middle of the movement. These chords will return in the finale

stops.hear: A broad, singing tune in the violins, warm and hopeful
The singing tune, now in D major, louder and faster
stops.happening: The music turns to the major: the [[coda|coda]]

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: A last, loud D major chord, then straight on
stops.happening: No pause: the second movement begins

notice: Count how often the short, racing figure of the *Lebhaft* comes back. Schumann builds most of the movement from it.

movements.heading: Romanze: Ziemlich langsam
movements.summary: A short, sad song. An oboe and a solo cello sing it together, an unusual pairing. In the middle the winding melody of the first movement’s introduction returns, and a solo violin spins a delicate garland of fast notes around it.

mainIdeas.name: The song
mainIdeas.description: a simple, melancholy tune for oboe and solo cello together, over plucked strings.

mainIdeas.name: The garland
mainIdeas.description: a solo violin’s ornament of fast, light notes, in D major.

stops.hear: A soft chord, then oboe and solo cello sing a sad tune together over [[pizzicato|pizzicato]] strings
The winding melody from the beginning of the symphony
A solo violin weaves quick, light notes above the orchestra, in a brighter key
stops.happening: The violin garland, in D major

stops.hear: The oboe and cello’s sad tune again

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: A quiet chord that does not quite close
stops.happening: The music waits for the scherzo

notice: Listen for the oboe and cello together in the first bars: two very different sounds, an octave apart, blended into one voice.

movements.heading: Scherzo: Lebhaft
movements.summary: A heavy, stamping [[scherzo|scherzo]] in D minor, with strong accents on every beat. The [[trio|trio]] in the middle is its opposite: soft and flowing, and made from the violin garland of the slow movement. The trio comes twice, and the second time it fades away into the finale.

mainIdeas.name: The scherzo
mainIdeas.description: a loud, determined tune for the whole orchestra, rising in strides.

mainIdeas.name: The trio
mainIdeas.description: a quiet, gliding melody in B-flat major, the garland from the Romanze.

stops.hear: The whole orchestra, loud and stamping
Suddenly soft and flowing: the violins glide down in gentle waves
stops.happening: The trio, in B-flat major, built from the violin garland of the Romanze

stops.hear: The stamping scherzo returns
The soft trio once more

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: The trio thins out and the music fades, unresolved
stops.happening: No ending: the finale’s introduction is next

notice: Compare the trio with the violin solo in the Romanze. The notes are close, but the mood has changed from decoration to a calm song for the whole string section.

movements.heading: Langsam – Lebhaft
movements.summary: A slow, mysterious introduction in which the main theme of the first movement is heard again, slowed down, as if waking up. Brass chords grow louder, the tempo picks up, and the finale bursts out in D major with the same theme, now fast and bright. The symphony ends faster and faster.

mainIdeas.name: The awakening
mainIdeas.description: soft, shivering strings and a slow version of the first movement’s racing figure; brass chords answer it.

mainIdeas.name: The finale theme
mainIdeas.description: the first movement’s figure turned into a bright, energetic tune in D major, with a jumping, dotted rhythm.

stops.hear: Very soft, shivering strings; a slow version of a familiar figure rises from the low instruments
stops.happening: The slow introduction: the first movement’s theme returns, slowed down

stops.hear: Horn and trombone chords, growing louder and more expectant
stops.happening: The music gathers for the finale

stops.hear: Fast, bright and loud, in D major
A lighter, more playful tune
The themes are broken up and passed around the orchestra
The bright main theme returns at full strength
Faster, then faster again

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: A rush to the final D major chords

notice: In the slow introduction, listen for the first movement’s racing figure played slowly. Then hear it explode into the fast tune of the finale.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Wolfgang Sawallisch recorded all four Schumann symphonies with the Staatskapelle Dresden, one of the oldest orchestras in the world, in the warm acoustic of Dresden’s Lukaskirche in 1972. EMI later reissued the set among its “Great Recordings of the Century”.

threads.title: One symphony, one stream
threads.body: The four movements follow each other without a pause, and the themes keep returning in new forms. Building a whole symphony from a few shared ideas in this way is called [[cyclic-form|cyclic form]]; for its time the symphony was unusually tightly knit.

threads.title: Two versions
threads.body: The light, transparent score of 1841 and the fuller, more solid one of 1851 are both played today. Clara Schumann preferred the revision; Brahms preferred the original.

threads.title: Clara
threads.body: The symphony belongs to Schumann’s first year of marriage, the year he turned from piano music and songs to the orchestra.
